newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian air controllers deny near mid-air collision.
newsitem.headline: Indian air controllers deny near mid-air collision.

text.p: Air traffic controllers denied on Sunday that two planes carrying hundreds of passengers narrowly missed colliding near the Indian capital.

Officials had said earlier on Sunday that an Indian Airlines Airbus A320 and an Air-India Boeing 747 came within 300 metres (yards) of each other on Saturday evening as they approached New Delhi airport from Bombay.

But the Air Traffic Controllers Guild said the pilot of the Indian Airlines aircraft had misreported Saturday's incident, and that his plane was more than 17 miles (27 km) from the Air-India jumbo jet.
The guild said in a statement that the two planes were separated horizontally by more than 3,000 feet (915 metres).
It said the pilot of the Indian Airlines aircraft had misunderstood the data and reported a near miss to Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim, who happened to be on his flight.
"The pilot, under (the) wrong impression, misreported the incident to the honourable minister, who in turn ordered an inquiry into the incident".
"Both the aircraft were kept separated longitudinally by more than 10 nautical miles between them as is the requirement," the statement said. Ten nautical miles equals 18.5 km or 11.5 miles.
Earlier reports of a near miss had revived memories of the world's worst mid-air accident last November in which 349 people died.
On November 12, a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 freighter collided about 80 km (50 miles) west of New Delhi.
There were no survivors among the 312 people aboard the Saudi jumbo and the 37 on the Kazakh plane.
